title: Al-Musawwir, the Fashioner
hookLine: the Fashioner, who shapes every form
tomorrow: Amira snapped at Jordan again. how many sorries still count?

cards: Portrait mode on a phone blurs everything behind a face so the face stands out. Faces are what people point cameras at. So yesterday's question is a real one.
If al-Musawwir, the Fashioner, shapes every face, can a person paint one? Amira isn't the first to ask. Muslim scholars have argued it out, and the argument starts with the name itself.

teach.h: AL-MUSAWWIR: HE GIVES EACH THING FORM.
teach.b: Al-Musawwir is the Fashioner, the One who gives each thing its form. In Pickthall's words: "He it is Who fashioneth you in the wombs as pleaseth Him."
And the forms differ on purpose: "the difference of your languages and colours" is named among His signs.
One human family, many faces, one Fashioner. Now the two views. View one: don't make images of living beings.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: PAINT TREES, NOT SOULS.
teach.b: A hadith in Bukhari's collection warns image-makers of punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and when a painter told Ibn Abbas that pictures were his living, Ibn Abbas told him, in paraphrase: if you must, paint trees and things that have no soul.
Their best case: forming living things belongs to al-Musawwir, and a person shouldn't play at rivaling it. Trees are still a whole world to paint.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: THE WARNING IS ABOUT IDOLS.
teach.b: View two: other scholars read those warnings as aimed at images made for worship, or made to compete with Allah's creating, and they point to a report that Aisha played with dolls in the Prophet's house.
Their best case: a picture made to remember or to teach is neither an idol nor a rival, and the warnings were about those.
Both views agree on the center: every living form is His work, and no picture of a face is the face itself.
That's the line to tell a friend tonight: the debate about painting faces is a debate about how much honor to give the Fashioner.

how: Muslim scholars hold different views on drawing living beings: some avoid images with faces and keep to plants, patterns and calligraphy; others allow pictures made to teach or remember, never for worship.

games.q: your cousin says no faces in any picture, ever. you lean the other way. to be fair, what's her best case?
o: forming living things is the Fashioner's; Ibn Abbas told a painter to paint trees.
she doesn't like art much, so she found a rule that backs her up.
a verse of the Qur'an bans every picture of anything at all.
games.why: her view rests on hadith warnings and Ibn Abbas's advice. the other view answers that the warnings target idols and rivalry. both honor al-Musawwir; neither is a dislike of art.

practice: Hold up one hand and look at it for the whole sit: the lines across the palm, the creases at each knuckle, the curve of each nail. Turn it slowly, front and back.
No one drew this from a sketch you could see; in the Qur'an's picture, it was fashioned as He pleased.

wordCard.voice: Al-Musawwir: the Fashioner, who shapes every form, from the lines of a palm to the color of a face. The third of the three making names.

orig.note: Arabic: the Fashioner, who gives each thing its form. the third name in Qur'an 59:24.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: shaped by him, every face on every street. That's three making names in three days.
